strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful geometric problem: extracting meshes faithful to expressive neural implicit fields. Combining tetrahedral barycentric encoding with a ReLU MLP preserves continuous piecewise-affine structure, providing a sound basis for analytic extraction without the trilinear assumptions used by TropicalNeRF.

The grid-aware extension of edge subdivision is a useful algorithmic contribution. Region indicators, barycentric masks, and explicit neighbor tables provide concrete machinery for handling intersections across multiple encoder resolutions. Relevant prior encoders and analytic extraction methods are acknowledged.

Table 4 provides strong evidence of surface fidelity: mean absolute field residuals are approximately 8×10^-8, with angular differences rounding to zero. Applying Marching Cubes to the same trained networks makes this comparison particularly informative.

Evaluation covers 500 Thingi10K meshes, 100 ABC meshes, and five Stanford models. Reconstruction accuracy is competitive with HashGrid, and the preconditioning ablation improves Thingi10K Chamfer distance from 1856 to 1722. Reported extraction times of 1.42–4.56 seconds also suggest practical utility for the tested configurations.
weaknesses: The central claim of exact recovery is stronger than the supplied correctness argument and validation. Appendix A.1 establishes affine interpolation, but does not establish completeness or correct connectivity of the full extractor. Section 4.6 leaves face construction largely to a citation, while the handling of coincident boundaries, redundant constraints, and numerical tolerances remains unclear. SSDF, VSDF, and AD only evaluate the returned surface; even perfect scores cannot rule out missing components or holes. Explicit correctness conditions and completeness/topology tests are needed.

The preconditioner derivation contains a substantive inconsistency. Equation (34) identifies a nonsymmetric-under-axis-permutation matrix as the average over all six tetrahedra. For the subdivision in Figure 2, those tetrahedra are coordinate permutations of one another, so their average metric should already be permutation invariant; the displayed matrix instead corresponds to an individual tetrahedron orientation. Equation (35) appears to recover the appropriate symmetric average, but this needs correction. Moreover, whitening three selected barycentric coordinates is not by itself evidence of whitening the learned feature Jacobian or improving optimization conditioning; convergence or directional-sensitivity measurements would strengthen that interpretation.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete relative to the claims. Table 5 reports only the proposed method, without runtime or peak-memory comparisons against competing extractors. The Large setting already constructs 35 million vertices and 130 million edges using a very small MLP. Section 4.5 also explicitly expands a product of per-level neighbor counts. Scaling with encoder levels and network width, and any pruning used to control these costs, should be established.

Several empirical conclusions exceed what the comparisons isolate. Table 3 changes both the learned representation and extraction method, so TropicalNeRF's degradation at lower resolutions cannot be attributed specifically to extraction heuristics. Table 6 uses different approximate references for different extractors and gives no uncertainty for small Chamfer differences. It also reports inconsistent Medium-setting vertex counts for the same proposed extractor and labels an apparent MT256 row as MC256.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the useful supplementary lookup tables. The manuscript omits numerical values for the extraction tolerances, hash-table sizes, optimizer and learning-rate settings, exact dataset subsets, and detailed SDF sampling proportions. These omissions matter particularly for reproducing near-machine-precision extraction and interpreting modest reconstruction improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: extracting meshes faithful to expressive neural implicit fields. Combining barycentric tetrahedral encoding with a ReLU MLP preserves continuous piecewise-affine structure and provides a sound foundation for analytic extraction.

The main algorithmic contribution goes beyond replacing interpolation: region indicators, barycentric masks, and neighbor lookup tables extend edge subdivision to the encoder’s multi-resolution polyhedral complex. Relevant antecedents are acknowledged.

Table 4 provides strong evidence of surface fidelity. Across three datasets, the proposed extractor achieves surface and vertex SDF residuals around 8×10^-8 and angular differences rounding to zero, substantially outperforming Marching Cubes applied to the same networks.

Experiments cover 500 Thingi10K meshes, 100 ABC meshes, and Stanford models. Table 1 shows competitive reconstruction accuracy, while Table 2 supplies a useful preconditioning ablation. The reported extraction times and supplementary implementation details also support practical potential.
weaknesses: The central claim of exact zero-set recovery is insufficiently established for the complete algorithm. The supplementary proofs establish affine interpolation and cell convexity, but not completeness or correctness of the combined adjacency and face-reconstruction procedure. Section 4.6 largely delegates triangulation to prior work, without explaining degeneracy handling. Moreover, SSDF, VSDF, and AD only evaluate the returned surface: even zero values cannot exclude missing components or holes. A correctness argument with explicit assumptions, supplemented by coverage and topology checks, is important for this claim.

The preconditioning rationale needs correction and stronger justification. For the six tetrahedra in Fig. 2, the average reduced-coordinate metric is already the symmetric matrix in Eq. (35); Eq. (34) instead gives a single tetrahedron’s metric. This error does not invalidate the final whitening matrix, but the broader interpretation is also under-supported: the metric omits the fourth barycentric coordinate and does not incorporate learned feature differences, so whitening it does not establish isotropic feature sensitivity or improved optimization conditioning. Training-stability claims lack convergence or variability measurements.

Experiments do not fully separate representation improvements from extraction improvements. Table 1 compares both different networks and different extractors; it lacks the proposed network extracted with MC512 and evaluated against ground truth. Table 3 similarly attributes resolution-dependent differences to TropicalNeRF’s extraction heuristics without reporting the corresponding HashGrid-plus-MC results at each resolution. Table 4 convincingly isolates surface residuals, but not the claimed reconstruction benefits.

Efficiency evidence remains limited. Table 5 reports only the proposed method’s runtime and memory, with no matched baseline measurements. The Large configuration already constructs 35 million vertices and 130 million edges and uses 8.01 GB, despite employing only four encoding levels and a width-12 MLP. Scaling to additional levels or larger networks is untested, particularly relevant because Section 4.5 explicitly forms products of neighboring-region configurations.

Table 6 is difficult to interpret as evidence of superior extraction accuracy: each baseline family uses a different sampled pseudo-ground-truth surface, and independently sampled Chamfer distance can obscure small extraction errors. There are also reporting inconsistencies: the proposed Medium mesh has 73,851 vertices in two blocks but 82,050 in the DC block, despite ostensibly using the same trained network. The MT block contains an MC256 label. These need clarification, although the label correction alone is minor.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. The manuscript omits numerical extraction thresholds, optimizer and learning-rate settings, batch size, hash-table size, and selected dataset identifiers or selection seeds. No repeated-run variability is provided, making modest differences such as 1718 versus 1737 on Stanford difficult to assess. Overall, the promising construction and strong residual measurements bring the paper close to acceptance, but the exactness and comparative-evidence gaps favor borderline rejection.

strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution: it combines an expressive multiresolution tetrahedral encoder with analytic extraction from ReLU networks. Barycentric interpolation preserves continuous piecewise-affine structure, addressing a concrete limitation of trilinear encoders without reverting to plain MLPs.

The extraction framework contains substantive algorithmic work beyond changing the interpolation rule. Encoder-aware region indicators, barycentric boundary masks, neighbor lookup tables, and initial-skeleton construction adapt edge subdivision to the multiresolution polyhedral complex. Relevant prior encoders and analytic extraction methods are appropriately acknowledged.

Table 4 provides strong evidence of surface fidelity across three datasets. Surface and vertex SDF residuals are approximately 8e-8, with angular discrepancies rounding to zero. Applying Marching Cubes to the same trained networks makes this comparison particularly informative.

Reconstruction quality remains competitive while enabling analytic extraction. Table 1 reports the best Chamfer distance on the evaluated Thingi10K and ABC subsets, and Table 3 shows substantial improvements over TropicalNeRF at smaller encoder resolutions. The preconditioner ablation improves Thingi10K CD from 1856 to 1722.

The reported implementation is practically promising: extraction takes 4.56 seconds and 8.01 GB at the Large setting on a V100. The supplementary derivations and explicit neighbor tables provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The unconditional claim of exactly recovering the entire zero-level set is stronger than the supplied validation. SSDF, VSDF, and AD measure agreement only on the extracted surface; they cannot detect missing components. The supplement establishes the affine representation but does not establish completeness of the full extraction procedure. Explicit correctness assumptions, handling of degenerate intersections and numerical thresholds, and tests of component coverage or watertightness would strengthen the central claim.

Scalability is demonstrated only for four encoder levels and a small decoder with three width-12 hidden layers. The Large initial skeleton already contains 35 million vertices and 130 million edges, while Section 4.5 enumerates products of neighboring configurations across levels. No scaling study over level count or decoder capacity, or comparative extraction runtime and memory measurements, establishes the broader efficiency claim.

The preconditioner derivation needs clarification. Equation (34) labels an asymmetric matrix as the average over all six axis-permuted tetrahedra, although this average should already have the permutation symmetry introduced in Equation (35). Moreover, the metric uses only three barycentric coordinates and does not establish its relationship to the learned feature Jacobian or optimization conditioning. The empirical improvement is useful, but claims of training stabilization are not supported by convergence or variability measurements.

Some experimental interpretations exceed what the comparisons isolate. Table 3 changes both the representation and extractor, so its improvements cannot be attributed specifically to avoiding TropicalNeRF's extraction heuristics. Table 6 uses different sampling-based pseudo ground truths, making its CD values indirect measures of fidelity; it also inconsistently reports the Medium vertex count for the same proposed extractor as 73,851 and 82,050. These issues warrant clarification, although Table 4 independently supports high self-consistency.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete: the manuscript does not specify numerical extraction thresholds, actual hash-table sizes, optimizer and learning-rate settings, or selected dataset identifiers. No repeated-run variability accompanies the relatively small Large-setting reconstruction gains. Overall, the central contribution supports a slight preference for acceptance, but the completeness, scaling, and derivation concerns prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: combining expressive grid-based SDF representations with analytic extraction of their zero-level sets. Under Algorithms/General, the contribution is valuable even without consistently outperforming HashGrid in reconstruction accuracy.

The central construction is technically well motivated. Barycentric interpolation preserves the CPWA structure, and the region indicators, barycentric masks, and tensorized skeleton construction provide a concrete extension of existing edge-subdivision methods to multiresolution encoders.

The experiments distinguish representation accuracy from extraction consistency and cover 605 shapes across three datasets. Table 4 provides strong evidence of numerical field–mesh agreement, with surface residuals around 8×10^-8 and negligible reported normal differences. Ground-truth reconstruction accuracy remains broadly competitive with HashGrid.

The supplement strengthens the practical case through runtime, memory, adaptive-extractor, and larger-MLP comparisons. Large-setting extraction takes 4.56 seconds on Stanford, including skeleton construction. The discussion also usefully quantifies skinny triangles rather than concealing this limitation.
weaknesses: The unconditional exact-recovery claim is stronger than the supplied correctness argument and evaluation. The proofs establish affine structure and cell convexity, but do not establish completeness and correct connectivity of the full extraction procedure. Sections 3.2–4.6 leave degeneracies, coincident boundaries, and final polygon reconstruction insufficiently specified. SSDF, VSDF, and AD sample only the extracted mesh, so low values cannot rule out omitted components or incorrect topology. A correctness statement with explicit assumptions, supplemented by coverage and topology checks, would substantially strengthen the central claim.

The preconditioner derivation has a concrete inconsistency and an insufficiently justified interpretation. Equation (34) labels a single-tetrahedron metric as the average over all six tetrahedra; for the stated subdivision, that average is already the symmetric matrix in Equation (35). More substantively, the metric uses only three barycentric weights and omits the dependent fourth weight and learned feature differences. Its connection to actual encoder sensitivity and optimization conditioning therefore requires justification. Table 6 supports an empirical accuracy benefit, but does not demonstrate the claimed training stabilization.

Some efficiency and compactness claims are overstated. The advertised 10×–20× vertex reduction is supported by the illustrated Small setting, but Table 5 gives 280,929 vertices for Ours-Large versus 426,394 for MC512 and 688,562 for DC512. The paper should qualify these claims by network setting and report comparable accuracy–size–runtime tradeoffs. Table A4 also omits the operating depths and refinement criteria needed to interpret the adaptive baselines.

Several reconstruction improvements are modest and lack uncertainty estimates. For example, Table 1 reports 1722 versus 1763 on Thingi10K, while HashGrid performs better on Stanford. Repeated training runs or paired per-shape distributions would clarify the robustness of these differences. Table 5's extractor-specific pseudo-ground-truths and finite-sample Chamfer distances also make its small numerical differences difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive geometric appendix. Numerical thresholds, optimizer and learning-rate settings, batch size, exact SDF sampling distribution, dataset subset identifiers, and complete hashing configuration are not specified. These details particularly matter for reproducing near-machine-precision extraction and assessing numerical robustness. Overall, the promising construction and substantial empirical evidence narrowly favor acceptance, but the exactness and preconditioning claims need tighter support.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, the paper offers a useful contribution: combining a multi-resolution tetrahedral encoder with a ReLU MLP preserves continuous piecewise-affine structure while providing substantially better representation capacity than the tested plain MLPs. Extending analytic extraction to this representation is a meaningful advance beyond merely changing the interpolation rule.

The experiments distinguish reconstruction accuracy from agreement with the learned field. Across 605 shapes from three datasets, Table 4 reports surface and vertex residuals around 8×10^-8 and angular discrepancies rounding to zero. Comparisons against sampling-based extraction on the same trained network provide persuasive evidence of substantially improved field consistency.

Reconstruction accuracy remains competitive with HashGrid: Table 1 shows modest improvements on ABC and Thingi10K, with a modest disadvantage on Stanford. The supplementary comparisons include larger analytic-marching networks and adaptive extractors, strengthening the empirical case beyond the main baselines.

The tensorized skeleton construction, explicit neighbor tables, runtime and memory measurements, and quantitative discussion of skinny triangles provide useful implementation detail and acknowledge a meaningful practical limitation. Together, the representation and extraction results support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The unconditional exact-recovery claim is stronger than the algorithmic specification and validation establish. Sections 3.2 and 4.6 describe subdivision at neuron boundaries followed by selecting vertices with near-zero output, but do not clearly specify the final subdivision by the scalar output's zero plane. Threshold handling, coincident boundaries, and face reconstruction are also insufficiently detailed. Moreover, SSDF, VSDF, and AD evaluate only the returned mesh: they cannot detect an omitted component of the network's zero set. Explicit extraction assumptions, completeness tests, and degeneracy handling would materially strengthen this central claim.

The preconditioning derivation contains a concrete inconsistency. Equation 34 identifies a nonsymmetric-in-the-axes matrix as the average over the six tetrahedra in Fig. 3, although those tetrahedra are related by axis permutations and their average should already have the symmetric form given in Equation 35. The later whitening construction can still be meaningful, so this does not invalidate the extraction contribution. However, the metric also omits the fourth barycentric weight and learned feature differences; its relationship to actual optimization conditioning needs justification. Table 6 demonstrates an accuracy benefit, but does not directly establish training stability or reduced directional sensitivity.

Scalability is demonstrated only for four encoder levels and a three-layer, width-12 decoder. Section 4.5 explicitly enumerates a product of levelwise neighbor counts and an exponential number of ReLU sign perturbations. Table A2 already reports 35 million initial vertices, 130 million edges, and 8.01 GB peak memory for the Large setting. Scaling experiments over levels and decoder capacity, or a complexity discussion explaining practical pruning, are needed to delimit the efficiency claim.

Several accuracy and mesh-efficiency conclusions need tighter qualification. Large-setting CD improvements over strong baselines are small and have no uncertainty estimates. Table 5 uses independently sampled, extractor-specific pseudo ground truths, without measuring the sampling floor, making differences of a few CD units difficult to interpret. The advertised 10–20× vertex reduction is also setting-dependent: in the Large setting, Table 5 shows approximately 1.5× relative to MC512 and 2.5× relative to DC512.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the substantial supplement: numerical thresholds, optimizer and learning-rate settings, precise sampling proportions, and selected dataset identifiers are not specified. The project-page field is blank. These omissions are particularly relevant because numerical boundary decisions are central to reproducing the reported extraction fidelity.

strengths: The paper makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution: combining an expressive multiresolution tetrahedral encoder with analytic extraction of a ReLU network’s zero-level set. The novelty lies in the grid-aware extraction machinery and its integration, rather than barycentric interpolation itself.

The central mathematical premise is sound: barycentric interpolation is affine within each tetrahedron, and multilevel concatenation followed by a ReLU MLP preserves continuous piecewise-affine structure. Region indicators, barycentric masks, and explicit neighbor lookup tables provide a concrete approach to extending prior edge-subdivision methods.

The experiments convincingly demonstrate field–mesh agreement. Table 4 reports surface residuals around 8×10⁻⁸ and angular discrepancies rounding to zero across three datasets. Applying sampling-based extractors to the same trained network is an appropriate control; the adaptive-extractor comparisons in Table A4 strengthen this evidence.

Extraction fidelity does not require a large sacrifice in reconstruction accuracy. Tables 1 and 3 show competitive performance against HashGrid, including better Chamfer distance on ABC and Thingi10K. The evaluation covers 605 shapes, and supplementary comparisons include larger plain ReLU networks, runtime, memory, and triangle quality.

The implementation appears practically promising: the Large configuration averages 4.56 seconds for extraction on Stanford, including skeleton construction. The paper appropriately acknowledges skinny triangles and quantifies this limitation rather than equating exact field agreement with universally superior mesh quality.
weaknesses: The strongest exactness claims exceed what is explicitly established. The supplementary proofs establish the representation’s affine structure, but do not establish completeness and robustness of the full extraction procedure. Surface-sampled residuals and normal agreement cannot detect missing components. Sections 3.2 and 4.6 should explicitly describe processing the final scalar output’s zero plane, handling coincident boundaries and degenerate cells, and reconstructing faces. Completeness or topology checks and tolerance-sensitivity experiments would strengthen the central guarantee.

The preconditioning argument needs correction and more careful interpretation. Equation 34 identifies an asymmetric matrix as the average over all six tetrahedra, although the stated tiling and common corner reference should yield an axis-permutation-invariant average; Equation 35 appears to supply that average. Moreover, the metric uses only three barycentric weights, omitting w₀, and therefore is not directly the sensitivity metric of the complete interpolated feature vector. Table 6 supports an empirical improvement, but does not establish the claimed training-stability mechanism.

The reconstruction gains over HashGrid are modest and mixed: Table 1 improves from 1854 to 1758 on ABC and 1763 to 1722 on Thingi10K, but worsens from 1659 to 1718 on Stanford. Repeated runs or paired per-shape statistics would help establish these smaller differences. Likewise, Table 2 alone cannot attribute TropicalNeRF’s low-resolution degradation to extraction heuristics because both the learned representation and extractor change.

Scalability remains bounded by the tested configurations. All experiments use four encoder levels and a small three-layer, width-12 decoder; the Large skeleton already contains 35 million vertices and 130 million edges, with 8.01 GB peak memory. The multiplicative neighbor expansion in Section 4.5 warrants complexity analysis or scaling experiments before extrapolating to substantially larger networks or scenes.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: numerical thresholds, optimizer settings, batch size, exact sampling proportions, and selected dataset identities or seeds are not specified. Table 5 also reports different vertex counts for the same Medium analytic extraction depending on the comparison block, which should be clarified. These issues limit independent verification but do not negate the main empirical result.
